1560: They gave a magnificent speech, promised nothing at all, and left holding what wasn't theirs.
1561: Charming beyond words, they agreed to absolutely nothing, and departed with a thing that belonged to us.
1562: They spoke grandly about friendship, committed to no single part of it, and walked off with an item of mine.
1563: A dazzling toast, a warm speech, zero commitments, and one of our treasures gone before the dessert.
1564: They flattered the whole room, signed nothing, and somehow left carrying something that was not their own.
1565: Their speech moved us to tears. Their hands, meanwhile, moved something valuable quietly out the door.
1566: They pledged boundless cooperation, agreed to nothing specific, and left carrying a little more than they came with.
1567: Grand words, a firm handshake, no actual agreement, and one missing piece from the reception hall.
1568: They charmed everyone present, pledged nothing binding, and took a keepsake that was never offered.
1569: A beautiful address about unity, followed by a very quiet exit with an object that wasn't theirs.
1570: They spoke of great friendship, would not put a word of it on paper, and pocketed something of ours.
1571: So charming I forgot to notice they had agreed to nothing and left with more than they came with.
1572: They gave the finest speech I have heard in this hall, committed to none of it, and left with a treasure.
1573: Warm, eloquent, evasive — and by the end, one of our things had quietly become one of theirs.
1574: They toasted our future together, promised nothing about it, and left holding what I had not given them.
1575: A grand performance of goodwill, no signatures anywhere, and a valuable item mysteriously absent after.
1576: They charmed the envoys, dodged every single commitment, and departed with something taken off the mantel.
1577: Their speech promised everything and delivered no part of it — except the part where our treasure vanished.
1578: They flattered us, they toasted us, they agreed to nothing, and they left carrying what was ours.
1579: The speech dazzled everyone; no one noticed it promised nothing, or that a treasure left with the speaker.
1580: They pushed their whole stack onto one number, won, and thanked me as if I had arranged it personally.
1581: They bet more in one hand than my table sees in a week, then tipped me twice that for luck.
1582: They won six times in a row, blew a kiss at the wheel, and left while it was still spinning.
1583: They asked me to raise the table limit, then complained the limit was too easy to reach.
1584: They tipped every dealer in the room, bowed to the cards, and vanished on the best streak I have seen.
1585: They played only the highest bets, won most of them, and told the dice they had been magnificent.
1586: They filled both hands with chips, called it a modest start, and never sat back down.
1587: They won a mountain of chips, gave half to the staff, and left the rest as a monument.
1588: They insisted the whole table stop so everyone could watch them win, then they did.
1589: They ordered the biggest chips we had, stacked them into a tower, and admired it more than the game.
1590: They doubled their bet each round, won each round, and applauded the wheel for its taste.
1591: They tipped me enough to retire, then asked me to remember the exact moment they walked away.
1592: They wagered a fortune on a single card, turned it over themselves, and took a bow.
1593: They cashed in more than the vault likes to hold, and left mid-winning, just to make a point.
1594: They kept winning, kept tipping, and left the table while it was still their turn.
1595: They told me to keep the change, and the change was heavier than the tray.
1596: They won so steadily they began apologizing to the other players, then kept right on winning.
1597: They asked me to explain the odds, listened politely, and then ignored them into a fortune.
1598: They played one glorious streak, tipped the room, and walked out as if leaving was the real trick.
1599: They won a small fortune, declared themselves the luckiest person alive, and left before I could disagree.
